AI Risk Assessment : Mitigating Risks in the Age of Generative AI

AI Risk Assessments & Global AI Regulations

Challenges of AI Risk Assessment

However, the allure of AI potential shouldn’t lead to lapses in understanding the risks these capabilities pose. Doing so is not only a regulatory requirement but also makes for good organizational practices.

Like any other technological leap, one key facet of challenges posed by AI is to understand and quantify the risks posed by AI. For businesses that hope to leverage the potential of AI, understanding any and all risks associated with AI is not simply a matter of regulatory compliance but of strategic importance. How they chart this course will have a lasting financial, operational, and reputational impact.

Whether it’s Morgan Stanley cracking down on the use of ChatGPT by its staff citing possibilities of hallucination while generating convincing outputs that are factually incorrect, Samsung banning its staff from using any GenAI tools after reports of multiple sensitive IP code being uploaded to such platforms, or the Dutch “toeslagenaffaire” scandal, where thousands of Dutch citizens had incorrectly been penalized by the tax authorities for suspected child care benefits fraud using a self-learning algorithm, these episodes echo the aforementioned problems of both inexperience and lack of a clear framework for responsible usage.

An AI risk assessment is designed to be a highly comprehensive and dynamic exercise that evolves apropos to the AI landscape and the unique needs of the businesses themselves. It not only helps identify all relevant risks an organization may be subject to but aids in the development of the strategies best poised to mitigate these risks.

AI poses significant risks and challenges for organizations hoping to implement it within their existing operations. The most significant and immediate risks of such an endeavor include:

AI models require extensive training on training sets to be functional. Often, such datasets contain personal and sensitive data. If not appropriately managed and protected, such data can be vulnerable to all manner of risks, such as breaches, unauthorized access, and misuse, which can result in privacy violations, corporate sabotage, and identity theft. Hence, it is critical for organizations to adequately encrypt and deploy appropriate access controls on all such data that is to be used as part of a training dataset.

AI Risk Assessments & Global AI Regulations

As AI continues to expand in both capabilities and operations, it has become increasingly important for organizations to conduct regular and comprehensive risk assessments to ensure the safe use of such capabilities while ensuring adherence to global AI regulations to the best of their ability.

While this is easier said than done owing to the diverse nature of global AI regulations in addition to their sheer number, these regulations serve as critical frameworks that allow organizations a foundation to build upon when addressing the unique risks posed by AI developments. Additionally, such assessments are vital in helping organizations balance innovation with affording appropriate protection for their customers’ digital rights.

While different AI regulations will require organizations to undertake a variety of assessments and measures to ensure compliance, risk assessment provisions are one of the few cornerstones of each of these regulations.

An effective AI risk assessment constitutes a thorough and rigorous process where all AI models, systems, and capabilities deployed within an organization are evaluated to identify and mitigate any potential risks across different domains, such as security, privacy, fairness, and accountability.

Bias Assessment - Addressing the issue of bias within AI systems and models, specifically the input datasets, to monitor for any discrepancies in the form of discriminatory elements that may lead to potential bias in the generated outputs.

Algorithmic Impact Assessment - Focusing on the operational aspect of AI, specifically the generated outputs such as decision-making processes, data usage, and recommendations.

AI Impact Assessment - Evaluating the broader implications of the use of specific AI systems and models while taking into account any and all social, ethical, and environmental factors that ought to be considered.

AI Classification Assessment - Determining the categories of AI systems and models currently in use within the organization. These should be classified on a (low-medium-high) scale depending on their intended use and potential impact on the organization itself.

Challenges of AI Risk Assessment

While AI risk assessments are a critical tool that can be of tremendous help to organizations, they come with a host of challenges. These include the following:

Not only does this vagueness affect the ability to address issues of effectiveness and efficiency appropriately, but it also leaves organizations relying on estimates when assessing the risks posed by these systems and models.

Legal frameworks and risk assessment methodologies are being developed that can help organizations appropriately address the challenges that AI presents but these challenges are constantly evolving. The frameworks and methodologies are developed following a laborious and comprehensive process, highlighting how certain technologies and developments still need to be more regulated or sufficiently scrutinized.

This section elaborates on certain best practices an organization can rely on when carrying out an AI risk assessment:

Once an organization has appropriately classified all AI models, it can proceed to evaluate each model for the various risks it may be exposed to. Doing so is not only an effective way to comply with various global regulatory requirements but can help in identifying and mitigating the following risks:

Once an organization has an appropriate understanding of all AI models in-use as well as the unique risks associated with them, they can then proceed to connecting AI models to the relevant data sources, data processing paths, vendors, potential risks, and compliance obligations. Doing so not only helps create a foundation for AI risk management processes but also allows for continuous monitoring of all data flow.

This allows for a more in-depth context around the AI models in use within the organization while also establishing mechanisms that facilitate proactive measures to mitigate, or at the very least, minimize, any privacy, security, and ethical risks before they materialize.

With robust data and AI controls, organizations can thoroughly curate model inputs and outputs, ensuring they can identify and counter any of the aforementioned risks.

AI Adoption and Risks: 2023 marked a significant advancement in AI technology, particularly in Generative AI, which has become increasingly adopted in the business world. While AI presents substantial economic

AI Risks and Challenges: The main risks associated with AI include AI model risks (such as model poisoning, bias, and hallucination), prompt usage risks (prompt injection and DoS attacks), exfiltration risks, sensitive data risks, data leakage, and non-regulatory compliance. These risks necessitate comprehensive risk assessments to mitigate potential negative impacts on financial, operational, and reputational aspects of businesses.

AI Risk Assessment Importance: Regular and comprehensive AI risk assessments are essential for identifying relevant risks and developing strategies to mitigate these risks. Understanding AI risks is crucial for regulatory compliance and strategic business planning.

AI Risk Assessment Provisions: Effective AI risk assessments involve evaluating AI models, systems, and capabilities to identify and mitigate potential risks across security, privacy, fairness, and accountability domains. This includes bias assessment, algorithmic impact assessment, AI impact assessment, and AI classification assessment.

Best Practices for AI Risk Mitigation: Organizations should conduct AI model discovery, risk assessment, data & AI mapping and flows, and establish robust data & AI controls to manage and mitigate risks associated with AI use. This includes classifying AI models, identifying potential risks, connecting AI models to relevant data sources, and establishing controls for model inputs and outputs.

Yes, one of the most direct and immediate benefits of an AI risk assessment is that it can promptly identify potential sources of bias within all datasets, processes, or algorithms in use within an organization. Corrective measures can then be implemented as deemed necessary.

An AI risk assessment will typically focus on AI and machine learning-related systems, such as bias, data quality, and ethical considerations. A traditional IT risk assessment focuses on the broader IT security and operational risks, such as network security and data breaches.

Consider a standard week of schooling: teachers are buried in essays, research papers, homework, and whatever else students turn in, waiting for the teacher’s careful reading and considered helpful feedback, about their essays, research papers, and other assignments. Grading takes place after lesson planning, family outreach, and administrative work, often extending deep into the evening. This is a fairly common dilemma and one that has many teachers searching for smarter, faster methods to help alleviate grading burdens and fatigue The AI grading tools available today, for teachers, help teachers navigate their significant workload, provide consistency in grading, promote academic integrity, and simply provide an experience while giving feedback that offers a balance between human teacher grading and AI support. Rather than teachers spending precious hours of time searching for errors or anomalies in text submitted by their students, technology can be the first layer of analysis for the teacher. This makes AI grading for teachers important.

Quetext’s AI Detector and Plagiarism checker are an example of grade-analysis as a portion of the continuum of the teaching to the learning experience. Teachers can use this technology to help the quickly determine if a submission contains text generated by AI, or if a student’s submission is unoriginal – all with insightful information provided. The grading process is quicker and more trustworthy than ever.

What Is AI Grading? (And How It Works)

AI grading describes the use of artificial intelligence in assessing student work­ primarily writing assignments­ and involves assessing student work on writing quality, structure, clarity and originality. Teachers can leverage AI systems that automatically scan and analyse text, instead of manually reviewing each sentence, for fast data-informed insights.

These technologies are powered by machine learning and natural language processing (NLP) algorithms that can assess students’ essays, reports and homework assignments. They identify patterns of writing, assess grammar and coherence, flag potential issues, and even recognize content that appears to be AI-generated or plagiarized. For example, with AI grading, a teacher can get quick insights into the writing of students, and at the same time check for originality by accessing Quetext’s AI Detector and Plagiarism

Checker. This allows educators to promote academic integrity, without adding to an already heavy workload. As of today, AI Grading, in conjunction with checks for originality, is commonly a feature in modern classrooms and allows teachers to be more efficient while fostering students to produce work that is authentic and high quality.

Why Teachers Are Turning to AI Grading Tools

Teachers are now facing unprecedented levels of pressure ,­larger class sizes, tightening grading deadlines, and growing bureaucratic demands. As grades pile up, it is sometimes difficult to achieve fair and consistent evaluations in equal time. Meanwhile, while the advent of AI writing tools allows students to create writing samples that might fool even the most well-trained eye, schools are becoming increasingly conscious of being able to recognize AI-generated text. Schools need trustworthy solutions to protect academic integrity.

Additionally, in the journey towards a more data-driven and transparent grading process, schools want to achieve grading that is both efficient and fair for all students. AI tools help solve this problem by providing objective insights that inform evaluative judgement while achieving consistent assessment, countering the risk of biases by making teachers aware of process errors.

That is why educators are turning towards Quetext. With the support of its AI Detector and Plagiarism Checker, Quetext supports educators in the grading process when that would normally not be achievable, and ultimately guarantees that each assignment is original, authentic, and prepared according to classroom norms. While AI tools can expedite the grading process­ they protect the integrity of education, the role of education today.

Top Benefits of AI Grading for Teachers

The biggest value of AI grading tools is their capability to review large quantities of work instantaneously. Rather than reading each paper and examining every detail, AI takes care of repetitive tasks such as assessing mechanical errors, organization, flow of ideas, and basic logical progression. It takes hours off of the routine grading that teachers do not have. Once this work is done, educators will have the time to focus back on what is most important – positive interactions with students, enhancing individualized feedback, and engaged planning for the lesson.

Human grading can be subjectively skewed by being tired, biased, or just by the mood one is in. AI provides consistency by evaluating each student via the same level of assessment across the student submissions. Regardless of the subjectivity or criteria in grading, the outcome of AI grading will create a more objective, transparent process that ensures every student is evaluated against the same rubric.

AI grading tools allow students to receive immediate feedback through detailed reports that outline strengths, weaknesses, and opportunities for growth. The tools provide more than just grades. Educators can assess student work to see a cohesive pattern across multiple students. For example, if several students struggle with thesis editing or transitions, the educator can modify instruction. Feedback is given much quicker than the educator could otherwise promote.

As AI writing tools are increasingly adopted, instructors find themselves facing another wave of challenges: essays created by artificially intelligences, undetected paraphrasing, and more subtle types of unoriginal content. Quetext takes this challenge head-on. With the AI Detector and Plagiarism Checker, teachers can confirm whether students’ work are original compositions on the spot. The tools serve educational purposes to assist teachers in: • Recognizing AI-written content • Catching poor or non-existent citations • Preventing academic dishonesty • Adhering to fair assessment for all students AI grading along with originality checks would go a long way in safeguarding the integrity of classrooms in today’s digital world.

Many AI-based grading tools consist of scoring systems that involve a smart grading model, or perhaps based on rubrics that organize classroom grading in a manner that prevents bias – or at least reduces it. So much the better for the rest of us who are feeling by the time a student assessment on an essay-based subject, or throughout the semi-subjective process of hybrid assessments. AI-generated scoring, as appropriate, will help take the pressure off the normal concerns about maintaining grading quality over the time and impact on workflow.

How AI Grading Tools Work (Step-by-Step)

AI grading may sound complicated, but the process is refreshingly uncomplicated and teacher supported. Here’s how it usually pans out:

The assignments-essays, reports, reflections, or homework-are uploaded into the AI grading system for analysis.

The limitations of AI are largely technical. AI systems can misinterpret authorial re-styling (unique writing style) or disregard subtler intent of expression. Teachers should always review AI’s insights and its suggested scores for precision and validity. AI should be understood as a grading assistant, but never as a substitute to educators. AI-assisted tools, like Quetext, work with detection and preliminary analysis; teachers presume the emotion, expertise and judgement needed to evaluate a student’s real understanding. Intentional uses of AI improve grading while firmly embedding the educator at the forefront of academic evaluation and assessment.

Quetext is the perfect tool for teachers who want to be as fair and honest as possible when grading assignments. Quetext’s powerful combination of AI Detection and Plagiarism Checking allows teachers to verify the work is original and authentically written before they begin the grading process. The major benefits of Quetext are: • Instantly recognizes AI text • Identifies unoriginal and/or unreferenced passages • Clearly formatted originality reports for easy comprehension • A clean, easy-to-use dashboard that seamlessly fits into classroom flow Now, teachers can grade with complete confidence that the assignment is indicative of a student’s real work before grades are derived.

AI and Auto-Grading in Higher Education: Capabilities, Ethics, and the Evolving Role of Educators

AI and Auto-Grading in Higher Education: Capabilities, Ethics, and the Evolving Role of Educators

Yuhan Gao Graduate Research Associate gao.2332@osu.edu

Yuhan Gao Graduate Research Associate gao.2332@osu.edu

AI and Auto-Grading in Higher Education: Capabilities, Ethics, and the Evolving Role of Educators

As artificial intelligence continues to reshape various industries, its impact on higher education, particularly in assessment, is becoming increasingly significant. Automated grading and AI-assisted evaluation tools are revolutionizing how instructors assess student work, streamline feedback, and manage large-scale courses. This article synthesizes recent research on the differences between auto-grading and AI grading, explores their respective strengths and limitations, and offers insight into how institutions are navigating this rapidly changing landscape.

Understanding Auto-Grading vs. AI-Assisted Grading

Auto-grading tools often called Automatic Assessment Tools (AATs), have been in development since the 1960s (Messer et al., 2024). These systems typically assess code or structured responses using static analysis (e.g., syntax checking, code similarity) or dynamic analysis (e.g., unit testing). Static approaches include abstract syntax tree analysis, control flow analysis, and code similarity detection. These tools check variable naming, code formatting, and programming constructs without running the code. Most dynamic AATs use unit testing or input/output testing to grade and give feedback. Dynamic approaches involve running the code to check if it behaves as expected. Tools like Carmen Speed Grader and H5P are examples used at institutions such as The Ohio State University. To implement a text-based AAT, instructors must provide detailed test suites and require students to follow specific structural conventions for accurate grading.

By contrast, AI-assisted grading powered by large language models (LLMs) and natural language processing (NLP) can evaluate complex, open-ended assignments such as essays or discussions. These models, like ChatGPT, leverage vast pre-trained datasets and use few-shot or zero-shot learning to assess submissions with minimal explicit programming (Flodén, 2025). Unlike AATs which are better at scoring multiple-choice questions, short answers, true/false questions and are less good at open-ended discussion questions, LLMs, natural language processing (NLP) and other AI-assisted assessment tools can be used to automatically grade more complex assignments including open essay questions, writing assignments, and providing detailed feedback on the texts, etc.

Capabilities, Limitations, and Ethical Considerations

Auto-grading systems excel at evaluating objective, well-structured tasks like multiple-choice, short answer, or programming assignments. However, they struggle with open-ended tasks, GUI-based assignments, and assessing aspects like readability or documentation (Messer et al., 2024). They often require manual grading supplements for larger, more nuanced projects.

AI-assisted grading, on the other hand, offers promising potential for large-scale, subjective assessments. Still, it introduces ethical concerns around bias, transparency, and fairness. Flodén (2025) and others argue that institutions must understand the risks of algorithmic bias and advocate for transparency in how AI tools are used in educational assessments.

Institutions like Northern Illinois University and MIT Open Learning stress the importance of disclosing AI involvement in grading, noting that students have a right to understand how their work is evaluated. While AI can be refined over time, its "black box" nature poses challenges for trust and accountability.

Universities across the U.S. are actively integrating both auto-grading and AI-assisted grading tools. Platforms like Gradescope, Crowdmark, and Akindi are popular for streamlining grading workflows and offering real-time feedback. Gradescope, in particular, is widely adopted by institutions including Cornell, Purdue, UC San Diego, Florida, Rutgers, and Indiana University.

The University of Miami showcases Gradescope’s AI capabilities, such as automatic answer grouping, auto-grading for specific question types, and compatibility with both online and traditional assessment formats.

While AI systems can process assignments at scale, ensuring their accuracy remains a key challenge. Biases can stem from outdated or unbalanced training data, affecting grading reliability especially in controversial or complex subjects (Wetzler et al., 2024). Studies show that AI often grades more leniently on low-performing essays and more harshly on high-performing ones, suggesting it should not yet be used as a standalone grading method (Wetzler et al., 2024). Flodén (2025) mentions that ChatGPT has been found to provide unreliable results such as incorrect answers, made-up facts, non-existent references and publications.

Nonetheless, human grading is not without bias. Grading inflation, subjective interpretation, and fatigue all influence instructor evaluations. While research studies acknowledge these issues, it still treats human scores as the benchmark for accuracy without critically questioning their reliability. If the accepted goal in human grading is to minimize bias, the same standard should be applied to AI. AI systems, unlike humans, can be refined, audited, and improved systematically. Rather than dismissing AI for its current limitations, it would be more productive to view AI as a tool in development. Thus, improving both AI and human grading in parallel is critical. Institutions are encouraged to adopt a hybrid model, combining human oversight with AI-generated feedback.

Despite advancements in AI, educators remain essential to the grading process. AI and auto-grading tools should be seen as supportive technologies and not replacements. Research by Flodén (2025) showed that while AI grading of essay exams yielded somewhat comparable results to human grading, teachers still expressed concern over student acceptance and AI’s limitations in assessing creativity or nuance. Wetzler et al. (2024) showed that AI grading has consistent bias. This pattern of proportional bias, along with generally low agreement between AI and human scores, suggests that generative AI is currently unsuitable as a sole grading tool, particularly for nuanced writing tasks that involve creativity and depth of thought. The study further affirms that AI is best used in formative assessments, where feedback can supplement human judgment rather than replace it.

Enhancing Equity, Efficiency, and the Future of Assessment

AI holds significant promise for improving grading efficiency and especially in large, online courses. Gnanaprakasam and Lourdusamy (2024) highlight how AI can personalize learning, manage thousands of assignments, and enable scalable instruction. However, such potential must be balanced with ongoing development to reduce bias, improve transparency, and ensure alignment with pedagogical goals.

Ultimately, realizing the benefits of AI and auto-grading in education demands a collaborative, multidisciplinary approach. Technologists, educators, students, and policymakers must work together to build assessment systems that are equitable, reliable, and trustworthy.

During my last year as a classroom teacher, I was tasked with grading 5,400 assignments. Here’s the math: 150 students x 4 quarters x 9 assignments (the number we were required to grade quarterly). Yes, some of those 5,400 were short quizzes or in-class presentations I could assess in real time. But because these were Honors and IB English language arts (ELA) classes, many other assignments were paragraphs or full-length essays. If I spent just ten minutes per essay per student, that added up to 25 hours of grading for a single assignment. By contrast, I had 7.5 hours of in-school prep time each week, and much of that time was absorbed by meetings, lesson planning, and family communication.

I loved teaching writing, but all those hours grading late at night and on the weekends snowballed into one of the largest forces that drove me out of teaching. “Set more boundaries!” I kept hearing. But nothing seemed skippable. Less planning time would’ve meant struggling through worse lessons, ignoring email would’ve meant missing updates from families and colleagues, and so on. I never figured out a way to streamline without losing something essential.

While my situation was perhaps extreme, it was hardly unique. Three-quarters of teachers who plan to leave identify “an unmanageable workload” as a key factor. Only 19 percent of teachers report working 40 or fewer hours per week during the school year (compared to 60 percent of otherwise similar working adults). And almost a third work 51 hours or more (compared to 9 percent of adult peers). Although it’s true that grading isn’t the only professional responsibility that teachers have outside regular hours, it’s high on the list for many.

With the advent of generative AI just months after I left teaching, the challenges of grading student writing ballooned, as students began submitting ChatGPT-authored work while schools scrambled to respond to the new technology. I was not sorry to have missed that shock to the system. But as I learned more, I became curious about how AI might ease teachers’ burden in other ways, especially by assisting with the time-consuming task of giving feedback on writing. Initially, I feared that AI would simply reward the most formulaic student writing or allow bias to pervade its judgments. Though I haven’t shed these concerns, I’m increasingly open to the possibility that, as long as there are humans who care about writing, we can teach AI to attend to the nuances of writing.

Earlier this year, I spoke with a high school ELA teacher who’s doing exactly that. She explained how she “put her brain” into her school’s AI program by feeding it assignment prompts, grading rubrics, past student work, and her own past feedback on student work. As it churned out scores and comments to students, the teacher gave the AI feedback to fine-tune it in accordance with her voice and instructional priorities. Even after months of this work, she still personally reviewed all student submissions and AI-generated feedback. And, she assured me, she was fully transparent about the process with her students.

This teacher isn’t alone. Though many educators remain wary of using AI for writing feedback, the use of platforms like MagicSchool AI for this purpose is becoming more widespread.

Yet this method of grading doesn’t seem portable across contexts. For starters, only an experienced teacher could provide such sophisticated bot-training. I imagine that it would feel more efficient to treat the AI much like a human teaching assistant, by reading the feedback closely during the first few attempts and thereafter trusting the assistant to stay on course, maybe checking a couple random samples periodically.
